lesson.title: Putting a Number on How Wrong You Were: Percent Error
lesson.summary: Percent error quantifies accuracy by comparing an experimental result to the accepted true value as a percentage, giving a standardized way to judge how well a measurement performed regardless of the size of the quantity involved.
lesson.body:
Accuracy and Precision introduced the idea that accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the true, accepted value, but that idea stayed qualitative, close or far, good or bad. Percent error turns that judgment into an exact number using the formula: percent error equals the absolute value of the experimental value minus the accepted value, divided by the accepted value, multiplied by 100 percent. The absolute value means the result is always reported as a positive percentage, since percent error measures the size of the discrepancy, not whether the experimental value came out too high or too low, though many lab reports note the direction separately as a diagnostic clue.

Consider a student determining the density of aluminum experimentally. The accepted density of aluminum, found in reference tables, is 2.70 g/mL. The student's experiment, using mass and water displacement measurements, yields an experimental density of 2.85 g/mL. Applying the formula: percent error = |2.85 minus 2.70| / 2.70 x 100% = 0.15 / 2.70 x 100% = 0.0556 x 100% = 5.56%, which rounds to about 5.6% given the precision of the input data. This tells the student that the experimental result deviated from the true value by about five and a half percent, a number that can be directly compared against other students' results or against a class target, such as requiring percent error under 5% for full credit.

Percent error is especially useful because it is a relative measure rather than an absolute one, which allows fair comparisons between experiments that would otherwise be impossible to judge side by side. Being off by 1 gram might be a huge, unacceptable error if the true mass was only 2 grams, since that represents a 50% error, but the same 1 gram discrepancy would be a trivial, excellent result if the true mass was 500 grams, representing only a 0.2% error. Because percent error divides by the accepted value before converting to a percentage, it automatically accounts for the scale of the quantity being measured, which raw absolute error in grams or milliliters cannot do on its own.

A low percent error is generally a sign of good accuracy, but it is worth remembering, building on the previous section, that percent error alone does not tell you anything about precision. A single measurement with low percent error might still have come from an imprecise instrument if that one result happened to land close to the true value by chance; the more rigorous approach is to run several trials, average them, and then calculate percent error on that average, which is far more representative of how the method actually performs than any single lucky or unlucky trial.

Finally, a large percent error is diagnostic information, not just a bad grade. If a percent error comes out unexpectedly high, it is a signal to look back at the experimental procedure for a source of systematic error, a miscalibrated balance, an air bubble in a graduated cylinder, a contaminated reagent, rather than simply attributing the result to random bad luck. Learning to read percent error this way, as a clue pointing toward a specific flaw in the method rather than a final verdict on the student's competence, is part of developing real scientific judgment.
